items.q: Why was the first week 39 freight accrual report rejected?
items.gold: It was filtered on planned delivery date instead of the actual delivery (POD) date, so five early-delivered shipments were missing.
items.answer:
- The first week 39 report (v1) was rejected by Ana Novak because it was filtered on the planned delivery date up to 25.09, the TMS default [13][14].
- The accrual needs the actual delivery (POD) date up to the cut-off. Early deliveries with planned dates of 26-28.09 are September costs, and the planned-date filter missed them [14][9].
- v1 showed 39 shipments totalling EUR 176,850. Ana asked Tom to rerun the report on the POD date [13][14].
- The corrected v2 showed 44 shipments totalling EUR 184,300, which was posted as document 1900004127. v1 is superseded and should not be used [12][17].
- The sources do not use the word "rejected"; this describes Ana's correction of the report.

judge.reason: The answer gives the key reference fact: v1 was filtered on planned delivery date instead of POD date, which missed early deliveries. Faithfulness fails because the cited sources [13], [14], and [17] are not in the provided list, and the v1 figures (39 shipments, EUR 176,850), the 'TMS default' claim, and the 26-28.09 planned dates cannot be verified from the visible sources.

items.q: Which steps does Ana follow for the weekly freight accrual?
items.gold: Get the TMS report, match in FBL1N, post with FB50 to G/L 4711000, and set the reversal for the 1st of the month.
items.answer:
Ana's weekly freight accrual steps:
- **Step 1, request:** Every Friday she asks Tom Hendriks for the TMS delivered-not-invoiced report, due by 12:00. It must include shipment, delivery, carrier, site and agreed freight amount [3]. On the last Friday of the month, the same request covers the month-end close [3][6].
- **Step 2, filter:** Filter on actual POD date up to the cut-off, not planned date. This has been required since 25 Sep 2026. The planned-date v1 report is superseded [3][2].
- **Step 3, clear:** Match each shipment in FBL1N. Invoiced items are cleared and drop out of the accrual [3][5].
- **Step 4, post:** Post the remaining total with FB50 to G/L 4711000, reversing on the 1st of the following month. The reversal is automatic [3][8][5].

items.answer:

- Tom Hendriks included deliveries 80419876 and 80419902 (Nordline, Hamburg) because the carrier confirmed delivery on 29.10 by email. Their POD was not yet in the TMS [1].
- Ana Novak approved inclusion on that carrier mail basis, matched them in FBL1N with nothing else open, and posted the EUR 201,950 accrual with FB50 to 4711000, reversing 01.11 [3].

items.q: Why did Antwerp choose a dispatcher check before loading instead of a check at the gate?
items.gold: The gate only checks driver ID and delivery number, and a dispatcher check before loading also avoids reloading a truck that cannot leave.
items.answer:
The gate check would not catch the actual problem. The gate only verifies driver ID and delivery number, so it would miss a missing dangerous goods declaration (DGD) [1][5].

- **Earlier and cheaper to fix:** The dispatcher checks before loading starts, so no UN 1263 pallet is loaded until the printed, signed DGD is in hand. This also avoids reloading a truck that cannot leave [1][5].
- **Decision history:** Marta Kowalska first proposed a gate check on 2 Oct [7]. Sofie Peeters proposed the dispatcher check on 5 Oct [1][5]. Marta agreed on 8 Oct, and the rule took effect on 12 Oct [2][9].
- **Root cause:** The DGDs existed in SAP but were never printed, because the print job went to the wrong office printer [1][11].

items.q: What caused the DGDs for the two UN 1263 shipments to be missing?
items.gold: They existed in SAP but were not printed because the print job went to the wrong printer in the office.
items.answer:
Both DGDs existed in SAP but were never printed. The print job went to the wrong office printer, so the signed DGDs never reached the shipment folder [5][9][2].

- Delivery 80451233 (UN 1263, 12 pallets), found 29 Sep 2026 [2][8]
- Delivery 80451290 (UN 1263, 8 pallets), found 30 Sep 2026 [2][8]

The DGDs were not missing from the system. Marta Kowalska had asked whether they were never created or only not printed [6], and Sofie Peeters answered that they were created but not printed [5]. The sources do not explain why the print job went to the wrong printer, or who created or requested each DGD [2][5].

judge.reason: States the reference's key fact: the DGDs existed in SAP but were not printed because the print job went to the wrong office printer. Dates, delivery numbers, and the Kowalska/Peeters exchange match the sources. The 'never reached the shipment folder' phrasing is a small inference but follows from the non-printing.
